Exercise 6.P1 — Easy: Safety is the minimum along a trajectory
      
        For state constraint $\bar g(x)=1-|x|$, a sampled trajectory visits $x=0,0.3,0.9,0.4$. Compute the smallest sampled margin. If it also visits $x=1.1$ between two samples, is the full experiment safe?
        Review if needed: Primer D: trajectories. Apply here: this module's explanation.
        Show hintApply $\bar g$ at every listed state. A minimum over samples need not equal a minimum over continuous time.
        
          Show worked solution
          The sampled margins are 1, 0.7, 0.1, and 0.6, so the smallest sampled margin is 0.1. At an intermediate state 1.1, however, $\bar g(1.1)=-0.1$, so the full continuous-time experiment is unsafe.A trajectory-minimum constraint must cover all relevant times. Sampling alone checks only the sampled states; a motion bound and an appropriate margin bridge the intervals. A safe final state, or even safe states at every recorded sample, is insufficient without that bridge.

reviewed_clauses.reason: The true continuous path supplies all printed states and exact individual margins. IsLeast concerns the actual finite sample range; a negative actual margin on the full path disproves all-time safety.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Samples/final state alone insufficient; speed/motion+margin bridges intervals.
hypotheses: Bounded speed throughout an actual differentiable sample interval and valid trajectory-margin Lipschitz/lower-bound assumptions when using the sufficient certificate.
reviewed_clauses.reason: The counterexample has safe recorded states and unsafe intersample margin. The general genuine displacement integral and Lipschitz transfer substantiate the stated remedy conditionally; no samples-only guarantee is inferred.

Exercise 6.P2 — Easy: Compute a backup ball
      
        A stored backup at state $x'=0.2$ has lower constraint margin $l=0.6$. Let $L_x=2$ and the between-sample motion allowance be $\Xi=0.05$. Compute its certified radius $r=l/L_x-\Xi$ and interval in a scalar state space. Check state 0.4.
        Review if needed: Primer B: sensitivity margins. Apply here: this module's explanation.
        Show hintThe motion allowance consumes part of the geometric radius.
        
          Show worked solution
          The radius is $0.6/2-0.05=0.25$, giving $[0.2-0.25,0.2+0.25]=[-0.05,0.45]$. State 0.4 is at distance 0.2 and lies inside the interval.The corresponding worst-case margin is $l-L_x(|0.4-0.2|+\Xi)=0.6-2(0.2+0.05)=0.1\ge0$. This is the certificate under the page's trajectory/Lipschitz assumptions. If $l/L_x-\Xi$ were negative, this backup would certify no states, rather than a ball with a negative radius.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: r=.25, literal interval[-.05,.45], membership.4, distance.2, negative radius excludes all states.
hypotheses: Scalar center.2,lower.6,L2,motion.05; the generic radius equivalence requires L>0.
reviewed_clauses.reason: Actual set equality with the closed interval and exact arithmetic prove radius and membership; nonnegative absolute distance gives empty negative-radius set.

hypotheses: True LipschitzWith2 g, .6≤g(.2), dist(activation,.4)≤.05, with g the backup trajectory constraint under the page assumptions.
reviewed_clauses.reason: The quantitative lower bound is derived for every allowable activation; the exact source fixture attains the printed guaranteed lower margin. The exercise does not ask a new whole global switching safety theorem.

Exercise 6.P3 — Easy: Turn a speed bound into a motion allowance
      
        A continuously monitored state has $\|\dot x(t)\|\le3$ in the chosen norm and is sampled every $\Delta t=0.02$. Bound its displacement between a sample and any time before the next sample. What allowance is needed if the interval doubles?
        Review if needed: Primer B: derivatives and rates of change. Apply here: this module's explanation.
        Show hintIntegrate the speed bound over at most one sampling interval.
        
          Show worked solution
          For $s\in[t,t+\Delta t]$, $\|x(s)-x(t)\|\le\int_t^s\|\dot x(r)\|dr\le3(s-t)\le3(0.02)=0.06$. Thus $\Xi=0.06$ is a valid allowance under the stated speed bound.If the interval doubles to 0.04, the allowance doubles to 0.12. The same lower constraint margin then covers a smaller set of starting states. The speed bound must hold throughout the interval, under the tested controller and any switching delay included in the model; a speed estimate at the sample alone does not establish this integral bound.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Actual chosen-norm displacement≤integral speed≤3 elapsed≤3 interval; .02/.04⇒.06/.12.
hypotheses: An actual path into any complete real normed space, differentiable throughout the closed interval; norm of its actual derivative≤3 throughout; sample≤time≤sample+interval.
reviewed_clauses.reason: Derivative measurability and integrability are derived from the bounded derivative, followed by the genuine norm-derivative integral inequality. The allowances are exact real rational arithmetic.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Larger allowance shrinks fixed backup region; speed at sample alone insufficient; bounds must cover controller and delay.
hypotheses: Nonnegative Lipschitz bound and increased allowance for inclusion; differentiability and uniform speed bound over the full interval used in the theorem.
reviewed_clauses.reason: Exact set inclusion proves coverage can only shrink. The smooth path1000t² has speed0 at sample0 yet displacement.4 at.02, exceeding.06. The general theorem includes any full delay interval; controller/delay advice names where its uniform premise must hold.

exercises.source_text:
Exercise 6.P4 — Easy: Why augmenting the state can be expensive
      
        A parameter grid has 100 points. A state grid has 10 bins in each coordinate. How many joint parameter-state pairs are there for two state coordinates? For six? Why does GoSafeOpt try to avoid learning a GP on that full product?
        Review if needed: Primer 0: Cartesian products. Apply here: this module's explanation.
        Show hintMultiply the number of parameter points by the number of state-grid combinations.
        
          Show worked solution
          With two state coordinates, the state grid has $10^2=100$ points and the product has $100(100)=10{,}000$ pairs. With six coordinates, there are $10^6$ state combinations and $100(10^6)=100{,}000{,}000$ pairs.The rapid growth comes from the Cartesian product: every extra coordinate multiplies the count by 10. GoSafeOpt keeps the learned GP on parameters and collects state backups along trajectories instead. This reduces the need for a full state grid; it does not remove the need to certify that those backups cover states reached during a global experiment.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Actual Fin100×(Fin d→Fin10) cardinality, both source counts and ×10 per added coordinate.
hypotheses: Exactly100 parameter-grid points and10 choices per independent coordinate; nonnegative natural dimension.
reviewed_clauses.reason: True Fintype cardinalities of the actual Cartesian product, rather than only unconnected arithmetic numerals, give10000 and100000000 and the all-dimension ×10 recurrence.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: GoSafeOpt learns parameter GP, collects rollout backups, and retains online backup coverage requirement.
hypotheses: This is a description of the named algorithm in the linked primary paper; no new empirical runtime or sample-complexity theorem is asserted.
reviewed_clauses.reason: Primary Algorithm1 updates parameter-indexed GP data and adds observed parameter/state rollout pairs to the backup set; Algorithm3 checks backup coverage during global exploration. This supports the stated architecture and requirement without attributing them to the Lean cardinality theorem.

Exercise 6.P5 — Medium: Unite backup regions without filling their gaps
      
        Two scalar backups certify intervals $[-0.4,0.1]$ and $[0.3,0.7]$. Which of states 0, 0.2 and 0.5 are covered? May the algorithm replace their union by the enclosing interval $[-0.4,0.7]$?
        Review if needed: Primer 0: interval unions. Apply here: this module's explanation.
        Show hintMembership needs one actual certificate. An enclosing interval can contain points covered by neither.
        
          Show worked solution
          State 0 is covered by the first interval, 0.5 by the second, and 0.2 by neither. The safe-state certificate is the union $[-0.4,0.1]\cup[0.3,0.7]$.Replacing the union by its enclosing interval would silently add the gap $(0.1,0.3)$ without a witness. Additional trajectory analysis might prove that some gap points are safe, but these two backup certificates do not. A geometric approximation of a certified set must remain inside that set if it is to preserve safety automatically.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Exact covered/uncovered source points, full gap exclusion, enclosing interval not a subset, arbitrary inner-set property preservation.
hypotheses: Exactly the two source closed intervals; an arbitrary safe predicate holds on the certified set and the approximation is a subset.
reviewed_clauses.reason: The actual union contains0/.5 and excludes.2, is disjoint from the entire open gap and does not contain the enclosing interval. Generic subset transfer proves automatic safety preservation for inner approximations. Source possible extra trajectory analysis is explicitly contingent advice, not a claim that any gap point is safe.

exercises.source_text:
Exercise 6.P6 — Medium: A suffix cannot have a smaller trajectory minimum
      
        A deterministic Markov closed loop under a fixed backup parameter has trajectory $x_a(t)$ from $x_0$, with constraint $g(a,x_0)=\inf_{t\ge0}\bar g(x_a(t))\ge0.2$. Explain why restarting the same controller at a visited state $x_a(t_1)$ has constraint at least 0.2. State what could break the argument.
        Review if needed: Primer 0: infima over sets. Apply here: this module's explanation.
        Show hintThe restarted path is a suffix when the state contains all information needed to determine future evolution.
        
          Show worked solution
          For autonomous deterministic dynamics with the same controller, uniqueness and the Markov state description give the restarted trajectory $x_a(t_1+s)$ for $s\ge0$. Its constraint is $\inf_{t\ge t_1}\bar g(x_a(t))\ge\inf_{t\ge0}\bar g(x_a(t))\ge0.2$, because the infimum is taken over fewer times.The argument can fail if restarting omits an internal controller state, the dynamics depend on an unrecorded clock, or switching does not actually reproduce the same closed loop. Markov means the stored state contains the information determining the future; merely naming a position as “state” does not ensure it.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Genuine restarted path and both-direction suffix margin set equality; true literal sInf suffix identity/inequality and retained≥.2.
hypotheses: The source complete autonomous deterministic Markov closed loop with fixed controller is represented by an actual start/restart flow law; time≥0 and actual original trajectory infimum≥1/5.
reviewed_clauses.reason: Restart law encodes the source complete-state deterministic evolution premise. Both directions establish equality with the original suffix; true real csInf monotonicity yields the result. Positive1/5 premise derives boundedness, so no additional undisclosed bounded-infimum assumption is used. This is not a theorem constructing arbitrary Lipschitz ODE solutions.

reviewed_clauses.source_clause: Omitted internal state/unrecorded clock or different loop can invalidate same-suffix argument.
hypotheses: Explicit full position×Bool/controller and position×clock autonomous flows satisfy true start/restart laws; omitting the second coordinate reconstructs a different full state.
reviewed_clauses.reason: The genuine full-state flows satisfy semigroup laws, yet identical observed positions with different hidden components have different unsafe futures. This directly substantiates the source failure possibilities; its switching caveat requires reproducing the same full loop, as stated in the restart premise.
